issues.legal_issue: A post-Constitution law made in violation of fundamental rights is void from its inception and cannot be treated as operative law.
material_facts: An earlier amendment had removed the right to seek eviction of a tenant from a non-residential building for the landlord’s own use.
The Supreme Court had held that the amendment’s distinction between residential and non-residential premises violated Article 14 and struck it down.
issues.conclusion: The amendment was void from its inception and could not be relied on as part of the law later extended to the territory.
issues.legal_principle: Article 13(2) makes a post-Constitution law that contravenes fundamental rights void to the extent of the contravention. Such a law is a nullity from its inception, rather than a valid law that later ceases to operate. The Court relied on Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Mahendra Lal Jaini v. State of Uttar Pradesh, and Harbilas Rai Bansal v. State of Punjab.

predicates.constitutional_validity_issue: A proceeding considers whether a law is constitutionally valid.
predicates.post_constitutional_law: The challenged law was enacted after the Constitution came into force.
predicates.fundamental_rights_infringement: The challenged law takes away or abridges a fundamental right.

issues.definition: When a constitutional-validity proceeding concerns a post-Constitution law that infringes fundamental rights, the law is void from its inception.

issues.legal_issue: The rent law extended to the territory permits a landlord to seek eviction from a non-residential building for the landlord’s bona fide own use.
material_facts: The dispute arose from an eviction proceeding concerning a shop-cum-flat let under a single tenancy, which qualified as a non-residential building under the applicable definition.
The territorial extension applied the entire existing rent law to the territory, subject to specified modifications.
The amendment that had removed the own-use ground for non-residential premises had been struck down as unconstitutional.
The rent authorities found that the landlord bona fide required the premises for his own use, and the appellate and revisional courts upheld that finding.
issues.conclusion: A landlord in the territory may seek eviction from a non-residential building for bona fide own use; the Court upheld the eviction orders.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2 and 3 of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction (Extension to Chandigarh) Act, 1974 applied the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949 to the territory. Because the amendment removing the own-use ground was void from its inception, the extended law was to be read without that amendment. The Court treated the legislation as an extension of the whole existing Act, not as incorporation of selected provisions, relying on M/s Punjab Tin Supply Co. v. Central Government and distinguishing the relevance of the incorporation principles discussed in State of Madhya Pradesh v. M.V. Narasimhan and U.P. Avas Evam Vikas Parishad v. Jainul Islam. It also relied on Harbilas Rai Bansal and Article 13(2) of the Constitution.

rule.if: territorial_extension_rent_proceeding and premises_nonresidential and amendment_previously_struck_down and landlord_bona_fide_own_use

predicates.territorial_extension_rent_proceeding: The proceeding concerns eviction under a rent law extended to a territory from elsewhere.
predicates.premises_nonresidential: The rented premises are classified as non-residential under the applicable law.
predicates.amendment_previously_struck_down: An amendment that removed the relevant eviction ground had previously been held unconstitutional and struck down.
predicates.landlord_bona_fide_own_use: The landlord genuinely requires the premises for the landlord’s own use.

issues.definition: If an extended-rent-law eviction proceeding concerns non-residential premises, the amendment removing the own-use ground has been struck down, and the landlord genuinely needs the premises for personal use, the own-use eviction ground is available.
